claims.claim: Page says Hobb drops information after the fact but in ways that point forward.
claims.source: M Harold Page, novelist, Black Gate craft dissection of Fool's Assassin, 2016
claims.quote: She drops information on us after-the-fact but in ways that point forward

claims.claim: Page says Hobb exploits the reader's knowledge of the genre instead of a point-of-view shift to keep the thriller plot alive.
claims.source: M Harold Page, novelist, Black Gate craft dissection of Fool's Assassin, 2016
claims.quote: She exploits the fact we know what genre we are reading

claims.claim: Page describes Fool's Assassin as a country house Gothic told from the point of view of its denizens.
claims.source: M Harold Page, novelist, Black Gate craft dissection of Fool's Assassin, 2016
claims.quote: a country house Gothic from the point of view

claims.claim: Hobb says the characters in her short fiction are people at the lower echelons of the economic strata.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed for The Geek's Guide to the Galaxy, reprinted in Lightspeed, April 2012
claims.quote: people who are at the lower echelons of the economic strata

claims.claim: Hobb says that in fantasy, people who work every day for a living on a tight budget can seem poor.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed for The Geek's Guide to the Galaxy, reprinted in Lightspeed, April 2012
claims.quote: people who actually work every day for a living

claims.claim: Hobb cites her own Alaskan upbringing, in which the family had to put food up for the winter, as the source of the survival economy in her work.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed for The Geek's Guide to the Galaxy, reprinted in Lightspeed, April 2012
claims.quote: we had to put that food up for the winter

claims.claim: Hobb, quoted by Hatch, says an antagonist simply has something they want to get done that outweighs the protagonist's aim.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, quoted by Tayan Hatch, Dragonsteel Books blog, 2024
claims.quote: They simply have something they want to get done
claims.page: Now I Believe Everything You Believe

claims.claim: Hobb, quoted by Hatch, says a writer must put a character's viewpoint on like a coat.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, quoted by Tayan Hatch, Dragonsteel Books blog, 2024
claims.quote: You have to put it on like a coat
claims.page: Now I Believe Everything You Believe

claims.claim: Hobb, quoted by Hatch, says the Farseer trilogy rewritten from Regal's point of view would make him a tragic hero.

claims.quote: he would be a tragic hero
claims.page: Now I Believe Everything You Believe

claims.claim: Hobb names coinage or money value, major religions and a calendar with seasonal names and year dates among the worldbuilding records she keeps.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, 'As You Intend To Be', robinhobb.com blog, 2020
claims.quote: coinage or money value, major religions, calendar with seasonal names

claims.quote: Joe is met in the tavern shortly before the disastrous river crossing

claims.claim: The article describes each Farseer chapter as beginning with a snippet of in-world text ranging from historical treatises to folklore and propaganda.
claims.quote: a snippet of in-world text ranging from historical treatises

claims.claim: The article says the dry, academic tone of an epigraph on Farseer glory is set against the unglamorous scene that follows.
claims.quote: the dry, academic tone of an epigraph

claims.claim: The article attributes Hobb's slow burn to dedicating thousands of words to the mundane details of the protagonist's daily existence.
claims.quote: dedicating thousands of words to the mundane details

claims.claim: Oliver describes the chapter epigraphs of Assassin's Apprentice as excerpts from a public document, largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins: Epigraphs and Negative Space in Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice', Mythlore 41.1 (2022), pp. 45-66
claims.quote: a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice
